body.text: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had an unmistakable air of confidence about him on October 23 as he took to the stage in Astana, Kazakhstan, before an eager audience of business executives, tech workers, political figures, and journalists.

In a nearly hour-long fireside chat with Kazakhstan’s Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang waxed effusive about the “incredibly visionary” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, praising his foresight in declaring AI development to be a “national priority.”

After Madiyev announced that Nvidia had invested an undisclosed sum in Higgsfield, an AI video-generation company that became Kazakhstan’s first unicorn in September 2025, Huang also heaped praise on the startup and its founders.

But above all, the microchip engineer-turned-billionaire executive was most bullish in describing the upward trajectory of the global AI industry and Kazakhstan’s potential to position itself at its center.

“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so many natural resources already. Instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform this energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said. “You’re going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”

On one level, Huang’s visit to Kazakhstan was just the latest stop on the barnstorming world tour the Nvidia boss first began in 2024 to sell the idea of “sovereign AI” to national leaders and statesmen.

But at another, it marked a meeting of minds and ambitions. The venerable chipmaker seeking to extend the global reach of its technology by powering next-generation data centers meets a resource-rich country hoping to turn its energy reserves into a competitive advantage in the AI economy. It’s a match made in heaven – or so it would seem.

Beyond this storybook partnership, however, lie significant challenges. Kazakhstan’s far-reaching AI plans call for billions of dollars in investment, expanded computing infrastructure, and a shift from supplying raw materials to producing higher-value digital services.

But experts say building and operating energy-intensive data centers will require not just abundant natural resources, but also a reliable electricity supply, the infrastructure to deliver it, and customers willing to pay for faraway computing capacity.
Coded in the Stars

For Nvidia, Kazakhstan is in some ways the ideal case study for its “Sovereign AI” strategy, which encourages governments to build domestic AI ecosystems around data centers, homegrown LLMs and local AI entrepreneurs, all powered by Nvidia chips.

Thanks in part to pitches like the one delivered by Huang in Astana, the strategy is quietly flourishing. In February, Nvidia’s chief financial officer said sovereign AI revenue had more than tripled to over $30 billion, and industry estimates suggest the company’s hardware underpins the overwhelming majority of sovereign AI language models.

But few countries have embraced Nvidia’s vision as fully as Kazakhstan. Since Tokayev pledged in 2025 to make the country a “fully digital nation” within three years, Astana has created an AI ministry, enrolled more than 650,000 students in AI training, and passed a comprehensive AI law, which entered force in 2026 amid the government’s “Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.”

This convergence was on full display in Astana last week, as Huang approvingly noted that Kazakhstan was “the first country that I’ve been to where the president declared the country to be an AI nation.” Madiyev, for his part, framed the government’s strategy in Nvidia’s terms, calling Huang’s “five-layer cake” AI economic model “the main pillar” of Kazakhstan’s digital strategy, and pitching the country’s mines and factories as a testing ground for Nvidia’s advancements in “physical AI.”

The more substantive partnership between the two, however, centers around the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, in northeastern Kazakhstan. There, beside the coal-fired Ekibastuz GRES-1, the country’s largest power plant, the government broke ground in January on Data Center Valley, a campus it hopes will eventually reach one gigawatt worth of computing capacity. (It was this project Huang had in mind when he called Kazakhstan a future “AI factory hub for all of Europe.”)

In June, Astana announced a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird, a U.S. cloud operator, and state-owned Kazakhtelecom to develop the site using Nvidia technology. Under the arrangement, Kazakhtelecom will provide power, cooling, and telecommunications infrastructure, while Firebird is set to finance the computing hardware.

More details about this investment became public last week, when Firebird signed an investment agreement with the government at the Akorda presidential palace, according to which the Data Center Valley site will be primarily used to generate computing power for international clients, with 10 percent of Firebird’s total GPU capacity to be allocated to Kazakhstani companies and government agencies. Under the agreement, the site will be powered by 45,000 high-end Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs, for which U.S. export licenses were announced last week.
For some experts, like Dr. Rustem Bigari, an AI and digital governance expert, this collaboration’s mutual appeal is apparent.

According to Bigari, Kazakhstan can offer globally competitive electricity prices, while data centers across the country are running low on capacity, meaning additional computing power is needed to fulfill the country’s AI ambitions, including developing Kazakh-language language models.

“We are offering the basic foundations that Nvidia needs,” Bigari told The Diplomat, adding that further investment in computing power would help Kazakhstan “become the main AI and cloud computing hub in the whole region.”

Similarly, Asad Bokhari, an assistant professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Public Policy, sees Nvidia’s arrival as vindication of the government’s broader digitalization campaign, and a signal that Amazon, Microsoft or Google “may also follow in its footsteps” by investing in the country.

“If the government of Kazakhstan was not prepared, all of the country’s resources would be useless for Nvidia’s data center plans,” Bokhari said, crediting the government’s institutional readiness. “But it is, so it’s a win-win for both sides.”
Critical Error!
But not everyone in the expert community was so impressed by Astana’s Nvidia-themed festivities last weekend.

“We looked at Jensen’s visit as basically just PR and marketing,” said Marat Beksultanov, a New York-based geospatial consultant who has studied the Data Center Valley project. “We weren’t expecting any breakthrough announcements.”

This is significant because, according to Beksultanov, the most important questions about the Data Center Valley remain unanswered. “There’s actually two extremely big issues,” Beksultanov told The Diplomat. “One is power, and then the other one is customers.”

Since 2023, Kazakhstan has consumed more electricity than it generated each year, typically making up the shortfall by importing power from Russia. Last winter, during a record peak, national grid operator KEGOC reported that the country had no spare generating capacity, leading to nearly 1,000 megawatts having to be imported on December 27.

The government had previously expected to achieve a modest power surplus by 2027. But the Data Center Valley’s first phase alone would see it consume more electricity at full capacity than that entire increased figure, according to Beksultanov’s analysis. Moreover, in mid-October an energy ministry official pushed back the energy self-sufficiency target to early 2028, months after the Data Center Valley is supposed to open.

“There’s a mismatch in the timeline,” Beksultanov said, adding that new data centers will also have to compete for power with the government’s existing industrial projects, including expansions in aluminum, steel, ferrosilicon and copper smelting capacity.
Yet even if Kazakhstan can ramp up its electricity generation, a potentially thornier question remains: who will actually use the Data Center Valley?

As Nazarbayev University’s Bokhari said, the announcement that 10 percent of the site’s computing capacity would be reserved for local universities, businesses, and public institutions offers some clarity on how Kazakhstan intends to benefit from the project. Bokhari said he expected the government to prioritize domestic users over exporting computing capacity abroad.

Nevertheless, the lion’s share of the Data Center Valley’s computing power is supposed to go to international customers, none of whom have been publicly identified yet. Russia and China, the geographically closest potential clients, seem likely to remain semi-permanently off-limits due to U.S. export controls, and – despite Huang’s confident predictions to this effect – Europe may not represent a realistic customer base, either.

Roughly 95 percent of Kazakhstan’s outbound internet traffic currently runs through Russia, raising questions of security and sanctions. And about three-quarters of the country’s electricity is generated by coal-powered plants.

“Maybe European customers will come en masse to Kazakhstan and start using their data centers tomorrow, but the [environmental, social, and governance] risks will likely pose a very strong barrier to business,” Beksultanov said.

The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable, inaugurated by Tokayev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in October, offers Kazakhstan an alternative route for international internet traffic to Europe via the South Caucasus. But with the cable’s commercial rollout and integration into wider networks still underway, how much traffic — if any — has already shifted away from Russia remains unclear.

The issue, ultimately, is that none of these problems stand to impact Nvidia’s interests or its approach. The company’s preferred business model is selling tools around the world to power the global AI revolution, which might explain its enthusiasm to partner with Kazakhstan’s government.

“Think about the gold rush,” Beksultanov said. “Nvidia is the guy who’s selling shovels. Would you expect that guy to say, well… this is a risk, you might not find gold? No, he would say business is good – go for it.”

Representatives from the AI ministry, Data Center Valley, and Nvidia did not respond to multiple requests for comment regarding the Data Center Valley project, its financing, power supply, future customers, or expected timeline of operations.
